article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) sought a response from the Union government on two separate petitions filed by a Phule-Ambedkarite and a former Kerala bureaucrat challenging government orders imposing the six-stanza Vande Mataram on the people.

A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant issued notice to the Centre on petitions filed by B.D. Borkar and former IAS officer Balakrishnan Sathyabhama Mavoji, both of whom have termed the six-stanza Vande Mataram a ‘divisive religious war song’ and a step towards theocracy.

The petitions argued that government orders had imposed a “sectarian prayer to particular goddesses of one particular religion as the National Song” which violated fundamental rights of religion and attracted the criminal law.

The petitions, represented by jurist and advocate Mohan Gopal, said a State compulsion expressed through two successive government orders on January 28 and July 9 would lead to the “unstated but undeniable consequence of irreversibly deepening communal division and conflict in India by outraging the religious and spiritual feelings of minority religions”.

Mr. Borkar has argued that the six-stanza version introduced by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee in his novel ‘Anandamath’ would promote enmity and conflict between different communities by advancing the supremacy of a dominant community.
The fabric of unity and harmony would be mutilated forever, he has said.

The plea said for 79 years, from independence until the issuance of these orders in 2026, the Union and State governments, public institutions and other groups had peaceably played and sung the “non-Anandamath” two-stanza Vande Mataram authored by Bankim Chatterjee in the early 1870s.
“This non-theistic song lauds the natural beauty of Mother Earth, describing the nation as a landscape and pays tribute to a non-deified motherland.
The song was treated in this period as the National Song even though not officially declared so,” the petition has said.
It said the stand-alone, two-stanza paean to the beauty of Mother Earth was authored by Chatterjee, and pre-dated and was independent of the subsequent six-stanza version found in the novel.
The petition has sought the court to intervene to quash the two orders, and stop any manner of compelling citizens, particularly school children, from singing or playing the six-stanza Vande Mataram.
It said the court could direct that the two-stanza, standalone version of ‘Vande Mataram’ alone be recognised, treated, performed and sung as the National Song.

stories.headline: Glacial Retreat—Part 2 : Five factors that make Kashmir's glacial lakes prone to outburst floods
stories.title: Glacial Retreat—Part 2 : Five factors that make Kashmir's glacial lakes prone to outburst floods
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 27: As glaciers retreat and new glacial lakes emerge across the Himalayan landscape, a scientific study has developed a risk-assessment framework to identify lakes in the Upper Indus Sub-Basin that may be more susceptible to glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs), a potentially devastating hazard capable of sending sudden surges of water, rocks and debris into downstream valleys. The study, published in Discover Geoscience by Suhail Ahmad and co-authors, assessed 775 glacial lakes using a combination of satellite imagery, glacier inventories and terrain modelling to estimate their relative susceptibility to outburst events. Rather than relying on lake size alone, the researchers examined a range of indicators linked to the processes that can trigger a sudden release of water. The assessment comes against the backdrop of substantial changes in the region’s glacial lake landscape. The study mapped 255 lakes covering 34.81 square kilometres in 1990, compared with 775 lakes spread across 37.72 square kilometres in 2025. This represents an increase of 520 lakes and an expansion of approximately 2.91 square kilometres in their combined area. The researchers cautioned, in effect, that the presence of a glacial lake does not automatically mean an outburst is imminent. The danger depends on a combination of physical conditions, including the lake’s connection to glaciers, the terrain surrounding it and the amount of water that can flow into it. To assess these differences, the study used a multi-criteria framework combining the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) with a Potential Risk Score Index (PRSI). The method assigns weights to different indicators and combines them into a relative susceptibility score, allowing lakes to be compared according to their potential hazard characteristics. “One of the most important indicators was the susceptibility of surrounding terrain to ice and rock avalanches. Such mass movements can enter a lake, displace water and potentially trigger an outburst,” the study reads. The researchers gave avalanche susceptibility the highest weight in their assessment, reflecting its importance as a recognised triggering mechanism for GLOFs. The study examined steep terrain within each lake’s upstream catchment, particularly slopes exceeding 30 degrees, alongside a critical reach angle of 14 degrees. These measurements were used as proxies for terrain where ice or rock avalanches could potentially reach a lake. “The size of the upstream watershed was assigned the second-highest weight. Their concerns centre on the combined workload arising from ward delimitation, voter-roll revision and the allocation of polling stations.
With November 12 as the deadline, parties argue that officials must verify voter movements, identify discrepancies and address pending appeals within a compressed timeframe.

stories.title: More than 100 people killed in Sudanese army drone attack on market, says Sudanese rights group
stories.summary: Shendi, Oct 28: More than 100 people were killed in a Sudanese military drone strike on a busy market in Nyala, the capital city of the South Darfur province in southwestern Sudan, said Emergency Lawyers, a rights group tracking violence in the country, in a statement Tuesday. The strike, which it says happened Monday evening, also injured 113 people. The group said many of those killed and injured were women and children. The group blamed the Sudanese military for the strike on the market, condemning the attack. “This massacre transformed a civilian marketplace into a scene of mass killing and injury and is an assault that threatens the lives of residents and compounds their suffering amid the ongoing war,” the group said in a statement. It called for an independent investigation into the strike. Doctors Without Borders, which is also known as Médecins Sans Frontières, or MSF, said earlier that 36 bodies arrived at its hospital in Nyala and reported seeing 150 injured in its emergency room. Nyala, the capital of South Darfur province, is controlled by the paramilitary group Rapid Support Forces, which has been fighting with the Sudanese army since 2023. Drone warfare has been a staple of this war but in recent weeks, a massive escalation of drone strikes by both the RSF and the Sudanese army has killed hundreds. Both warring parties have increasingly launched explosive-laden drones that, in multiple cases, targeted civilian infrastructure, including hospitals, dams, schools, markets and displacement camps. Drone strikes have become the deadliest threat to civilians in this conflict, according to the UN. The conflict has created the world's largest humanitarian crisis, with about 34 million people — almost two out of every three Sudanese — needing assistance, according to the UN. Sudan's war started in April 2023 when tensions between the military and the RSF exploded into open fighting in the capital, Khartoum, and spread across the country. Previous strike leaves parts of Sudan without power Large parts of Sudan's capital were without electricity for more than 12 hours Tuesday after a drone strike on a major power substation, according to an electric company official. The attack left hospitals and bakeries dependent on generators and limited water supplies across Khartoum. The state-run Sudanese Electricity Distribution Company acknowledged “serious damage and technical faults” to the distribution network and several main stations and power lines but didn't explain the reason in a statement. It apologized to residents across Khartoum state for repeated and prolonged outages. A company official, speaking to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media, said a drone attack hit the Al-Markhiyat transformer station in Omdurman, on the outskirts of Khartoum. He said it is the second to hit the station this year, blaming it on the country's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. The RSF has been at war with the Sudanese military for more than three years. Sudan's war began in April 2023, when simmering tensions between the military and the RSF exploded into open fighting in Khartoum and spread across the country. Deadly drone attacks across Sudan have been carried out by the two rival forces. But those attacks have become rare in Khartoum since the Sudanese military took control of the capital in May 2025, after years of brutal fighting between the military and the RSF. The UN has expressed concern over the use of drones across Sudan, saying they have been killing civilians, including children, and are disrupting essential services. The official who spoke to AP said technical teams are still assessing the damage, describing the strike as major. He estimated that 60 per cent of the power supply in the capital could be affected, predicting that water stations will be most affected. A resident living near the Al-Markhiyat transformer station in Omdurman said he heard a drone shortly before the blast. “At around 4:30 in the morning, on my way to dawn prayers, I heard the sound of a drone very close by, and just moments later a huge explosion, and the power went out,” Abdel-Hafiz Abdel-Mutaal told AP. “I saw fire burning at the transformer station.” The city descended into darkness after sundown. Adel Ali, a resident of south Khartoum, said he was without power and water for 17 hours. “My main concern is how to preserve my insulin supply which needs a fridge,” Ali, a diabetes patient, said. “Life without electricity is totally paralyzed, and a bread crisis is emerging as many bakeries have shut down.” He said this would drive the price of bread even higher. The electricity company, in its statement, said power rationing would be longer than usual in all areas until repairs are finished. It did not say when that would be. Technical teams were working around the clock to restore power, it added. The conflict has killed at least 59,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED, though aid groups say the true toll is likely higher. Over 67 per cent of the country's population is dependent on aid, while 825,000 children face acute malnutrition. The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, or IPC, a global food crisis monitor, warned last week that the “deteriorating humanitarian situation” across greater Darfur and Kordofan states is worsening, with food insecurity putting these areas at risk of famine. In a joint statement, over 30 countries, including the United States, United Kingdom and the European Commission, urged parties to the conflict in the country “to lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance.”

stories.title: Supreme Court needs transparent roster system, says former SC judge Oka
stories.summary: Former Supreme Court Judge Abhay Oka was speaking at a discussion on judicial accountability organised by the Campaign for Judicial Accountability and Reforms at the India International Centre in New Delhi

article_sentences: Former Supreme Court judge Abhay S. Oka on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) said the roster system followed by the Supreme Court needs to be overhauled to bring greater transparency to the allocation of cases and eliminate the scope for “manual intervention” in their listing.

Mr. Oka pointed out that several Benches of the Supreme Court are assigned the same categories of cases under the roster, making it difficult for a litigant to know which Bench a freshly instituted case would eventually be listed before.
The practice, he said, left room for human intervention in deciding where a case would be listed.
“The object of a roster is to ensure that the possibility of manual intervention in listing is ruled out.
But when the same subject is assigned to multiple Benches, a case can possibly go to five different Benches.
Who then decides which Bench a freshly filed petition goes before — the Chief Justice of India or an official in the Registry?
The fact remains that there is manual intervention in the listing of cases,” he said.

Mr. Oka was delivering the keynote lecture at an event on the “Accountability of Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts” organised by the Campaign for Judicial Accountability and Reforms (CJAR) in New Delhi.
The Chief Justice of India (CJI), as the “master of the roster”, has the administrative authority to constitute Benches and allocate judicial work among them.
Mr. Oka, however, said that the present system made the Supreme Court overly dependent on the office of the Chief Justice in matters of listing and allocation.
“The Supreme Court is too much of a Chief Justice-centric court.
The Supreme Court will become more favourable to litigants if it introduces a proper roster on a par with the High Courts, so that manual intervention by the CJI is ruled out,” he said.

stories.title: BJP wins all four Karnataka MLC seats in major blow to Congress
stories.summary: Bengaluru, Oct 28 : The BJP-led NDA has won all four Karnataka Legislative Council seats, marking a setback for Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar as Congress faced crushing defeat. While the ruling Congress did not win a single seat in the MLC elections, the BJP won three, and the Janata Dal (Secular) won one. The BJP won the North-East Teachers', the South-East Graduates', and the West Graduates' constituencies. Its ally JD(S) took the Bengaluru Teachers' constituency. In the South-East Graduates' seat, BJP's KM Suresh defeated the Congress' Shashi Hulikunte Mutt; in the North-East Teachers' seat, BJP MLC Shashil G. Namoshi defeated Congress candidate Sharanappa Mattur; and in the West Graduates' Constituency, the BJP's SV Sankanur won, defeating Congress's Mohan Limbikai. From Bengaluru Teachers' Constituency, JD(S) candidate A P Ranganath defeated five-time winner Puttanna. Speaking about the victory, BJP MLC Lingaraj Patil said, "Karnataka election results reflect public anger against the Congress government... People have rejected Congress due to alleged corruption, irregularities and unfulfilled promises." He further claimed that internal disputes within Congress have also affected the party's performance. "People are not affected by Congress' opposition to SIR, PM Narendra Modi and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar... People continue to trust PM Modi and the BJP," he said. This was the first election for the Karnataka Congress under its President B.K. Hariprasad, who is also an MLC. Currently, the 75-member Legislative Council has five vacant spots, 38 Congress members, 24 from the BJP, six from the JD(S), one independent and a chairman. The MLC elections were held on October 23 amid elaborate security arrangements to ensure peaceful and fair polling. A clash had broken out between Congress and BJP workers near a polling station at Ambedkar College in Nagarabhavi during polling for the Bengaluru Teachers' constituency. Former corporator Mohan Kumar was accused of verbally abusing people, following which the police intervened and erected barricades to bring the situation under control. --IANS

stories.headline: 4 ministers, 4 political journeys
stories.title: 4 ministers, 4 political journeys
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 27: From decades of electoral experience and party organisation to hard-fought constituency battles, Ali Mohammad Sagar, Saifullah Mir, Shamim Firdous, and Altaf Ahmad Wani (Kaloo) bring distinct political journeys to Chief Minister Omar Abdullah’s expanded cabinet. The four National Conference (NC) leaders represent different constituencies and generations of political contests, with experience spanning legislative service, ministerial responsibilities, and grassroots representation. As they take charge of their new portfolios, their political backgrounds offer a glimpse into the experience and electoral mandates they bring to the government’s developmental agenda. Ali Mohammad Sagar Ali Mohammad Sagar is a senior National Conference (NC) leader and seven-time legislator from Srinagar’s Khanyar assembly constituency. Sagar has built his political career through repeated electoral victories, organisational responsibilities within the NC, and ministerial service in previous National Conference (NC) led governments. His return to the cabinet marks another chapter in his decades-long political career. Sagar did his LLB from the University of Kashmir. His legal education preceded a political career spanning more than four decades. Sagar’s electoral journey began in 1983, when he was first elected to the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly from Khanyar. He subsequently won from the constituency in 1987, 1996, 2002, 2008, and 2014, before securing another victory in the 2024 Assembly election. His electoral record spans several distinct periods in J&K’s political history, with Khanyar remaining the centre of his legislative career. The 2024 Assembly election reaffirmed his position as the NC’s representative from the Srinagar constituency. Sagar received 14,906 votes, defeating independent candidate Sheikh Imran, who polled 4994 votes, by a margin of 9912 votes. Sagar has held senior organisational responsibilities in the NC and is often referred to as the party’s “crisis manager”. In June 2014, he was appointed the party’s General Secretary, succeeding Sheikh Nazir, who had held the position since 1996. Sagar previously served in the NC led government holding the portfolios of Works and Rural Development and Panchayati Raj. Saifullah Mir Saifullah Mir, a senior National Conference (NC) leader, represents the Trehgam assembly constituency of north Kashmir’s Kupwara district. A four-time MLA, Mir has previously represented the neighbouringKupwara constituency for three terms. A lawyer by profession and a former minister in the Jammu and Kashmir government, Mir returned to the Legislative Assembly in 2024 after winning the newly delineated Trehgam seat. He was continuously elected thrice from the Kupwara assembly constituency in 1996, 2002, and 2008 as an NC candidate. Following the delimitation of assembly constituencies, Mir contested the 2024 election from Trehgam and secured his fourth assembly victory. In the 2024 assembly elections, he won the Trehgam constituency, polling 18,002 votes, defeating People’s Conference (PC) candidate Bashir Ahmad Dar, who polled 14,376 votes, by a margin of 3626 votes. Mir did his LLB from the University of Kashmir in 1987. He previously also served in the NC-led government headed by Omar Abdullah. Mir was inducted into the ministry during a cabinet reshuffle in January 2013, alongside several other NC legislators. Shamim Firdous Shamim Firdous is a senior National Conference (NC) leader and a three-time Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) from HabbaKadal constituency in central Kashmir’s Srinagar district. She won the HabbaKadal assembly seat in 2008 and retained it in the 2014 and 2024 assembly elections. Firdous also chaired the Jammu and Kashmir State Commission for Women, holding the status of a Minister of State. She did her BA and LLB with Honours from the University of Kashmir in 1983. In the 2024 assembly election, Firdous secured 12,437 votes, defeating Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) candidate Ashok Kumar Bhat, who received 2899 votes, winning by a margin of 9538 votes. Beyond her legislative career, Firdous has held responsibilities within the NC Women’s Wing. Altaf Ahmad Wani Altaf Ahmad Wani (Kaloo) is a National Conference (NC) leader who represents the Pahalgam assembly constituency of south Kashmir’s Anantnag district. His political career is marked by an unsuccessful assembly election bid in the 2008 assembly elections, nomination in 2009 to the Legislative Council, and victories in the 2014 and 2024 Assembly elections. His electoral defeats and wins have featured repeated contests against a political heavyweight, Rafi Ahmed Mir, in Pahalgam. Wani won his first Assembly election in 2014, defeating Mir by a narrow margin of 904 votes in a closely contested Pahalgam race. He secured 25,232 votes, while Mir, the PDP candidate, received 24,328 votes. The result reversed the outcome of the 2008 election, when Mir had defeated Wani in Pahalgam. The two politicians would face each other again in the 2024 Assembly elections, making their electoral rivalry a recurring feature of Pahalgam’s political contest. In the 2024 assembly elections, Wani defeated Mir by a substantially larger margin of 13,756 votes, polling 26,210 votes, while Mir, contesting on the Apni Party ticket, received 12,454 votes. Wani did his Engineering in Mechanical Engineering from Islamia Institute of Technology, Bangalore, in 1995.
